questions.question: What is the main purpose of a cryptographic hash function like SHA-256?
options: Map arbitrary-length input bytes to a fixed-length digest
Encrypt data so only the key holder can read it
Sign data so anyone can verify who wrote it
Compress data to make it smaller for storage
questions.explanation: A hash maps bytes of any length to a fixed-size digest; it is not encryption or signing.

questions.question: When you hash a string in a program, what is the safest default practice?
options: Convert to bytes with an explicit encoding (e.g., UTF-8) and hash the bytes
Hash the language's string object directly with its default representation
Hash the hexadecimal text of the string for portability
Hash the string length and assume it uniquely identifies content
questions.explanation: Hashes are defined over bytes. If you start from text, pick an explicit encoding and hash the resulting bytes.

questions.question: In SHA-256, what is the digest size?
options: 256 bits (32 bytes)
128 bits (16 bytes)
512 bits (64 bytes)
1024 bits (128 bytes)
questions.explanation: SHA-256 outputs 256 bits, which is 32 bytes (or 64 hex characters).

questions.question: What does SHA-256 padding append at the end of the message?
options: A 64-bit big-endian encoding of the original message length in bits
A 32-bit little-endian encoding of the message length in bytes
A random salt so identical messages hash differently
A copy of the first 32 bytes of the message
questions.explanation: SHA-256 pads with 0x80, zeros, and then the original message length as a 64-bit big-endian bit count.

questions.question: How many 32-bit words are in one SHA-256 message block before expansion?
options: 16 words (from 64 bytes, big-endian)
8 words (from 32 bytes, little-endian)
32 words (from 128 bytes, big-endian)
64 words (from 256 bytes, little-endian)
questions.explanation: Each 512-bit block is 64 bytes, interpreted as 16 big-endian 32-bit words before expansion to 64.

questions.question: SHA-256 uses 64 rounds per block. What drives those rounds?
options: A message schedule W[0..63] and fixed constants K[0..63]
A randomly generated per-message nonce and a secret constant
A public-key signature over the block and a verifier key
A table of S-boxes derived from the encryption key
questions.explanation: Each round mixes the working state with one scheduled word W[i] and one fixed constant K[i].

questions.question: Attack scenario: a system uses token = sha256(secret || message) as an authentication tag. What is a realistic risk?
options: Length extension can let an attacker compute a valid token for message || extra without knowing secret
A collision can be found instantly for any chosen message
The secret key can be recovered from one token and one message
The hash output becomes reversible, revealing the full secret
questions.explanation: Merkle–Damgård hashes like SHA-256 can be length-extended when misused as a MAC; HMAC is designed to avoid this.

questions.question: Why do from-scratch SHA-256 implementations in Python frequently mask with 0xFFFFFFFF?
options: To force 32-bit modular arithmetic because Python integers do not overflow naturally
To increase the security level from 256 bits to 512 bits
To ensure the output is always ASCII for printing
To make the function constant-time on all CPUs
questions.explanation: SHA-256 is defined over 32-bit words. Masking simulates wraparound arithmetic after additions and rotates.
